coverage_note: 'The Intentionality of Sensible and Categorial Acts' (pp. 46-48) and II.1 sections I and II (pp. 125-136): the paragraphs carrying fulfilment vocabulary. Not read: the noema sections, 'A Hermeneutic Conception of Perception', 'Genesis of Objectivism…', 'Intentionality and Transcendence', II.1 section III, and the rest of the book.

units.claim: Because a perceptual statement contains forms with no counterpart in sensible perception, a categorial intuition is needed to secure its intuitive fulfilment.
units.quote: Hence the need for a categorial intuition to justify the truth of a perceptual statement, that is, to secure what Husserl calls its intuitive fulfilment.

units.claim: In the Investigations the empty component surrounding the intuitive givenness of a spatial thing is called the signitive content of perception, making thing-perception a mixed representation.
units.quote: In the *Investigations* this empty component of intuitive representation is called the *signitive* content of the perception of a thing

units.claim: Bernet rejects the signitive model of the unseen side: the empty component is the anticipation of a possible perception, not the interpretation of a sign.
units.quote: What I see of the thing without really seeing it is the object of a possible seeing: what is in question is the anticipation of an actual perception and a possible originary givenness, not the interpretation of a sign

units.claim: The Investigations' ideal of adequacy for external perception is said to be borrowed from internal perception, an ideal it is absurd for external perception to be guided by.
units.quote: Husserl seems for a moment to have forgotten that it is absurd to suppose external perception could be guided by an ideal belonging to the form of internal perception.

units.claim: Ideen I is said to understand the inadequacy of thing-perception as inseparability from an empty horizon of further appearances, so that a contradictory appearance always remains possible.
units.quote: A perception or appearance is called inadequate because it is inseparable from an empty intentional horizon containing the anticipation of other possible and complementary appearances of the same object.

units.claim: The continuous synthesis of appearances is a sensible synthesis of fusion or covering which, given the perceiver's interest, has the form of a process of intuitive fulfilment.
units.quote: Taking that interest and the teleological movement it imprints on the process into account, we discover that the continuous synthesis of appearances has the form of a process of intuitive fulfilment.

units.claim: Because the ideal of adequate givenness is inaccessible, the synthesis of fulfilment is at the same time a synthesis of emptying or unfulfilment, open to disappointment.
units.quote: The synthesis of fulfilment is therefore at the same time a synthesis of emptying (*Entleerung*) or unfulfilment (*Entfüllung*), since what is gained in intuitiveness by one appearance is lost by another.

units.claim: The unlimited process of perceptual fulfilment is also a process of transcendental constitution, the thing being the synthetic unity of its appearances.
units.quote: This unlimited process of perceptual fulfilment is also a process of transcendental constitution of the thing that appears

units.claim: Gurwitsch's identification of the thing-in-itself with the totality of its appearances is said to risk falling back into the Investigations' contradictory ideal of adequacy, against Ideen I's Idea in the Kantian sense.
units.quote: Gurwitsch would thereby lose the benefit of *Ideen I*'s analysis, on which the adequate givenness of the thing-in-itself is an Idea in the Kantian sense
